name: B&G Foods, Inc.

profile.description: B&G Foods manufactures, sells, and distributes a portfolio of shelf-stable and frozen foods and household products in the United States, Canada, and Puerto Rico. Brands include Crisco, Ortega, Cream of Wheat, Clabber Girl, Spice Islands, Dash, and College Inn (acquired 2026). The company divested the Green Giant U.S. Frozen business in Q1 2026 and cut its annual dividend 50% from $0.76 to $0.38 effective July 2026 to prioritize deleveraging.

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (0/3): B&G Foods has not launched meaningful new products or executed business model transformations in the last 5 years — the company has been in defensive mode, divesting Green Giant U.S. frozen operations and acquiring College Inn/Kitchen Basics broth to reshape its portfolio [1]. Revenue has declined from $2.16B in 2022 to $1.83B in 2025, a 5yr CAGR of approximately -2.7%. AI Deployment (0/2): No evidence of AI-powered products or AI-driven operational savings. The company is a traditional shelf-stable food manufacturer. Market Share (1/2): B&G holds meaningful positions in niche shelf-stable categories (Crisco cooking oils, Ortega Mexican foods, Spice Islands seasonings) but is not a category leader in any major food segment [1]. Pipeline (1/2): Q1 2026 showed encouraging signs with base business net sales growing 2.8% YoY, and the College Inn acquisition strengthens the Meals segment [1]. FY2026 guidance of $1.735B-$1.775B revenue and $275M-$290M adjusted EBITDA suggests early stabilization. R&D Intensity (0/1): B&G spends minimally on R&D — innovation function exists but spending is well below industry peers like General Mills or Conagra.

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (1/4): B&G Foods does not articulate a distinctive mission or purpose beyond operational and financial objectives — public communications focus on portfolio management, debt reduction, and adjusted EBITDA guidance rather than a vision of why the company exists [1][3]. Community Impact (1/2): B&G released an inaugural CSR report in January 2024 outlining environmental and social goals, including zero-landfill programs achieving 92% diversion rates at three facilities, pesticide risk mitigation with suppliers, and planting 150,000 trees in Mexico with a goal of 500,000 by 2028 [3]. However, charitable giving is not prominently quantified. Employee Retention (0/2): Executive departures raise concern — VP Andrew Vogel left in May 2026 amid a dispute over whether his exit was with or without cause, forcing CEO Keller to temporarily assume oversight of key business units [2]. Insider Buying (1/2): CEO Casey Keller received stock award grants in 2026, signaling compensation alignment, though no meaningful open-market insider purchases were identified [2].

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: B&G Foods' financial profile reflects a highly leveraged, low-margin packaged food company navigating a turnaround. D/E of 510% is above the 300% floor, scoring 0 — the company carries $2.0B in debt (over $1.5B maturing 2027-2028) against a $308M market cap [4][5]. ROE of -16.72% and profit margin of -4.23% are both below their floors, scoring 0 [5]. Revenue declined 3.74% YoY with a 5yr CAGR of approximately -2.7% [5]. Forward P/E of 6.25x is the sole bright spot among core metrics, scoring 1.0 [5]. The dividend was cut 50% from $0.76 to $0.38 effective July 2026 to prioritize deleveraging, bringing the FCF-based payout ratio to approximately 65% ($30.8M dividend vs $47.1M FCF), scoring 0.58 [1]. Consecutive years paid remains ~22 (since 2004 IPO), scoring 1.0 at 2x weight. But consecutive years growth = 0 and 5yr dividend growth CAGR of -16.74% both score 0. Liquidity floor cleared: 1.67M avg vol x $3.79 = $6.3M daily [5].

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): Packaged food manufacturing and distribution is a physical-world business that AI cannot substitute — making Crisco oil, packaging Ortega taco shells, and distributing to supermarkets requires physical plants, supply chains, and shelf space that software cannot replace [1]. Consumer food purchasing decisions are driven by brand loyalty, taste, habit, and shelf placement rather than digital disintermediation. The modest AI risk comes from AI-powered supply chain optimization and private label development by larger competitors (General Mills, Conagra) and retailers potentially widening the efficiency gap with smaller players like B&G. AI Opportunity (0/1): No evidence of AI revenue generation or meaningful AI-powered product innovation at B&G Foods.

infinite_game.summary: B&G Foods is playing a distinctly finite game — the company exists as a holding company for legacy shelf-stable food brands, optimizing for debt reduction and dividend maintenance rather than pursuing a Just Cause. The serial acquisition strategy that built the portfolio was financial engineering, not purpose-driven growth, and the current divestiture and dividend cut cycle reflects a company fighting to survive rather than one built to endure. The executive departure dispute in May 2026 and lack of articulated purpose reinforce the finite mindset.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (0/3): B&G Foods has no articulated Just Cause. Communications focus entirely on financial metrics — debt reduction, adjusted EBITDA guidance, portfolio optimization [1]. There is no vision of a future state that extends beyond 'managing a portfolio of shelf-stable food brands.' The Green Giant divestiture and College Inn acquisition are portfolio management moves, not purpose-driven strategy. This is a financial holding company for legacy brands.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): VP Andrew Vogel departed in May 2026 amid a dispute over whether his exit was with or without cause, forcing CEO Keller to temporarily assume oversight of key business units [2]. With 2,349 employees and a Glassdoor rating of 2.9/5 (33% recommendation rate), B&G's organizational culture shows significant trust deficits. Repeated restructuring, brand divestitures, and now a second dividend cut create persistent organizational instability.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): B&G Foods does not demonstrate an infinite competitive mindset — the company's strategy is about managing decline and optimizing a shrinking portfolio rather than using competitive pressure from General Mills, Conagra, or Campbell's to improve its offerings [1]. No evidence of management referencing learning from competitors.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): B&G is making painful strategic shifts — divesting the Green Giant U.S. frozen business and acquiring College Inn/Kitchen Basics to reshape the portfolio around higher-margin core brands [1]. The 50% dividend cut from $0.76 to $0.38 prioritizes deleveraging over income. These represent incremental adaptation driven by financial necessity, not a transformative pivot in service of a cause.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Cutting the dividend 50% to $0.38 and divesting Green Giant — the company's most recognizable brand — required leadership courage, even though the decisions were forced by $2.0B in debt with $1.5B maturing in 2027-2028 [1]. CEO Casey Keller has prioritized deleveraging over short-term market approval, setting realistic FY2026 guidance of $0.575-$0.675 adjusted EPS.

investment_thesis: B&G Foods is a deep value play in packaged foods trading at 6.25x forward earnings after a 50% dividend cut that clears the path for deleveraging [1]. Q1 2026 exceeded expectations with $408.9M revenue (beating $397.2M forecast) and $0.08 EPS (beating $0.05 forecast) [1]. FY2026 guidance of $1.735B-$1.775B revenue and $275M-$290M adjusted EBITDA reflects a streamlined portfolio. Base business net sales grew 2.8% YoY in Q1, suggesting early stabilization post-Green Giant divestiture. The reduced $0.38 annual dividend is covered by $47.1M FCF (65% payout ratio) and frees ~$31M annually for debt reduction [1]. The College Inn acquisition strengthens the Meals segment, and CEO Keller's focus on core brands (Crisco, Ortega, Spice Islands, Dash) could drive margin improvement.
thesis_continued: The bear case is severe. D/E of 510% with $2.0B in debt — over $1.5B maturing in 2027-2028 — creates existential refinancing risk against a $308M market cap [4][5]. ROE of -16.72% and profit margin of -4.23% indicate the business does not earn its cost of capital. Revenue has declined at a -2.7% 5yr CAGR as the portfolio shrinks through divestitures and consumers shift away from shelf-stable processed foods toward fresh, organic, and premium alternatives [1][5]. The 10% dividend yield (post-cut) still signals market skepticism — a second cut would likely trigger further equity price decline. The Vogel executive departure dispute and Glassdoor rating of 2.9/5 suggest cultural challenges that impair operational execution [2]. With $1.5B in debt maturing within 18 months, B&G's ability to refinance at manageable rates will determine whether this is a turnaround or a restructuring candidate.
key_catalysts: Base business stabilization — Q1 2026 revenue of $408.9M and 2.8% base business growth beat expectations, suggesting the portfolio restructuring is gaining traction [1]
Dividend cut frees ~$31M annually for accelerated debt reduction — if successful, improving the 510% D/E ratio could unlock meaningful equity value and reduce refinancing risk [1]
Margin improvement from exiting low-margin Green Giant frozen operations and focusing on higher-margin Spices & Flavor Solutions and Specialty segments with College Inn acquisition [1]
key_risks: Existential refinancing risk — $2.0B debt with over $1.5B maturing 2027-2028 against a $308M market cap; any deterioration in credit markets or operating performance could force restructuring [4][5]
Secular decline in shelf-stable food categories — consumer shift toward fresh, organic, and premium alternatives pressures volume and pricing power across B&G's entire legacy brand portfolio [1]
Cultural and leadership instability — Glassdoor 2.9/5 rating, VP departure dispute, and CEO wearing multiple hats signal organizational challenges that could undermine turnaround execution [2]
